A.explanation: Only a very small, massive, highly charged centre can repel a tiny fraction of $\alpha$-particles through angles greater than $90^{\circ}$ while most pass through undeflected.

B.explanation: Greater deflection of slower $\alpha$-particles shows the effect of electrostatic repulsion time, but does not by itself prove the charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

C.explanation: Unchanged kinetic energy shows the scattering is elastic, not that most of the atom is empty space with a dense central nucleus.

D.explanation: Dependence on foil thickness shows more atoms give more scattering, not that each atom has a small dense positively charged nucleus.

hints: Notice the contrast in the experiment between most alpha-particles passing straight through the gold foil and a tiny proportion scattering through large angles.
Recall that a large-angle deflection of a massive $+2e$ alpha-particle requires a very strong electrostatic repulsion from a small concentrated positive charge.
Ask which statement needs most of the atom to be empty space plus one tiny dense centre, rather than a spread-out charge or an elastic-collision detail.
walkthrough: Recall the set-up: a beam of positively charged alpha-particles is fired at very thin gold foil and most pass straight through with little or no deviation.
A spread-out positive charge, as in the plum-pudding model, could only produce weak electric fields and small-angle scattering.

A deflection through a large angle, including back-scattering, requires a head-on approach to a tiny region holding almost all the positive charge and mass, giving a very large repulsive force $F$ over a short distance.
The fact that only a tiny proportion suffer this fate shows that this massive centre occupies only a very small volume, with the rest of the atom being empty space.
The observation of rare large-angle deflections therefore directly implies a small dense nucleus. This is option A.
